claude.reason: Nero is sent, tests his fate with arrows and a child's verse, flees and converts: a sequence of events about a post-biblical figure, in scope.
Rabba's dictum embeds R. Yohanan's report of two Jerusalem families who set their meals at wrong times and were uprooted; two actions with a causal consequence.
R. Akiva and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter: betrothal, father's expulsion and vow, years of study, return with students; a full narrative.
An incident came before Rabbi of a man's offhand remark about captivity, and Rabbi ruled on it; a narrated event followed by a ruling.
Rav Pappa goes to write the ketubah, Yehuda bar Mareimar comes out to greet him and takes leave at the door; narrated actions of rabbis.
Mar Zutra's practice of scoring and writing the passage, an objection, and a ruling: a bare report of practice with no continuation, Jeff's own R-C5 case.
A maidservant in Pumbedita with whom people sinned, and Abaye responds about forcing her emancipation; an incident followed by a rabbinic response.
R. Ya'akov ben Dostai's one-time eyewitness account of walking in ankle-deep fig honey, with similar testimonies; the eyewitness-wonder type Jeff accepted for Ketubot 111b.
The death of Rabbi: the fast, the maidservant's prayer and jug, Bar Kappara's report, Rabbi's last prayer and the heavenly voice; a full narrative.
Giddul bar Re'ilai sends a get, his wife defers it, the agent reports and he blesses; a sequence of events with a response.
A bare report that Rav Zevid permitted (or himself did) first intercourse on Shabbat; nothing follows.
The Sages allot Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter a perfume allowance, she responds and they answer amen; an incident with a ruling and a reaction.
An incident came before Rabbi of a man's offhand remark about captivity with his mother, and Rabbi permitted her to marry a priest; event plus ruling.
A man contracts with his sharecropper for four waterings, then rain comes, and Rav Yosef and Rabba rule; a certain-man incident followed by rulings.
Geneiva, led out to execution, bequeaths 400 zuz to R. Avina and R. Zeira rules he may collect; segment 4 is the Gemara's legal reasoning, not the story.
At his death Rabbi summons his sons, they enter and he gives his last instructions; segment 3 is the Gemara's commentary on his words.
A woman taken as security in Ashkelon, distanced by her family, testified for by witnesses, and the Sages rule; an incident followed by a ruling.
Pure legal discussion of Shmuel's rulings and a mishna on vows; no event narrated.
A gentile announces Hasa drowned, Rav Nahman exclaims, Hasa's wife remarries and no one protests; events with a response and a legal inference.
Rav Kahana brings a get and asks Rav whether he must make the declaration; a halakhic query and answer with no conflict and nothing happening.
An incident in Shihin: a mustard branch breaks, yields nine kav, and its wood roofs a booth; a one-time wonder narrated as an event.
A certain man sold his property to go to Eretz Yisrael, did not go, and Rav Ashi ruled; the incident-plus-ruling shape R-C0 admits.
R. Elazar ascends to Eretz Yisrael, is ordained and seated on the intercalation council, responding at each stage; a sequence of events in his life.
Ulla visits Rav Yehuda and challenges him over his unmarried son; mostly dialogue with conflict but little action, and segments 4-5 are an interpolated exegetical exchange.
A certain man threw what he called a get among the barrels, a mezuza was found, and Rav Nahman ruled; an incident followed by a ruling.

A narrated incident ('a certain man was picking dates', a woman came and asked, he proposed betrothal, she answered) resolved by Rav Zevid's ruling; R-C0's incident-plus-ruling shape, with actions beyond speech.
A pauper comes to Rabbi Nehemya, eats lentils with him and dies, and Nehemya reacts; a sequence of events with consequence. The Gemara's gloss on his words is commentary but the incident is complete.
A man bequeaths property to Toviya, dies, Toviya comes, and Rabbi Yohanan rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
Rav Kahana is tempted, throws himself from a roof, is caught by Elijah and given dinars: full narrative about a rabbi (Elijah appearing to a rabbi read as in scope).

The rabbis sit and discuss a past practice of a city's slave-owners, cited only as a legal precedent to identify whose opinion it follows; the incident is alluded to, not narrated, and the scene is just a discussion.

Rav Hiyya Arikha's sister-in-law demands sustenance and her ketuba, sues him, he refuses to comply, a seizure order is written, and they appeal to Rava: an extended incident with conflict, actions and rulings.
A halakhic dilemma raised by Reish Lakish and left unresolved; no event.
A man sells land with a guarantee, a river is diverted through it, the case goes to Ravina and then Rava: incident plus rulings.

A man comes before Rabban Gamliel claiming he found his bride not a virgin, and Rabban Gamliel responds; an incident brought to a rabbi who answers it (the 'some say' variant is part of the same episode).
A hypothetical legal case from a baraita ('if they saw her...') with a tannaitic dispute; not an event that happened.
Speech only: Ravin bar Hanina states a halakha and Rav Hisda sharply objects; there is conflict but no event beyond speaking.
A Roman courts a woman, makes her ill with pomegranates, then cures her when she agrees to marry: a full sequence of actions with change.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba encounters Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying his grandson to synagogue, questions him, and thereafter changes his own practice: event, exchange and consequence.

First-person eyewitness incidents (food brought to Shmuel, he gave some to Rav Anan, averting danger); something happened and someone responded, though they are brief and cited as evidence, so this is close to the R-C5 line.
Rabbi Akiva moves the garden's entrance to block Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya from the tithe, and Rabbi Elazar reacts: action, conflict and response.
A habitual frame (Rabbi Hanina's weekly gift) followed by a one-time event: one day his wife delivers it and returns reporting what she heard.
Describes the habitual practice of two pious men and whether Elijah spoke with them; a custom with no one-time event following.
Segment 3 narrates an incident (witnesses wrote the wrong name in a woman's get) followed by Rav's ruling. Segment 2 only alludes to an incident, and segment 4 is legal objection, not story.
A scribe comes before Rabbi Ami confessing a defect in a Torah scroll he wrote; Rabbi Ami rules and defends the ruling to Rabbi Yirmeya: incident followed by ruling.
A legal dilemma and dispute, then Rav Nahman's rhetorical rebuke of Rav Anan within the argument; speech only, with no narrated event.
The martyrdom of the woman and her seven sons before the emperor: a full narrative about post-biblical figures, so in scope.
A brief report of the aftermath of an earlier case (the family remained, the Sages avoided it), mostly followed by the Gemara's explanation of their reasoning; nothing is narrated here on its own.
Rav Yosef plants mixed seeds, Abaye challenges him, and after a legal dialogue Rav Yosef retracts; this is mostly halakhic dialogue with conflict and implied change, but has little action.
A man sells his mother's ketuba, she dies without objecting, he contests the sale, and Rami bar Hama and Rava rule: incident followed by ruling.
A case comes before Rabbi Yohanan, Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yohanan disagree, and Reish Lakish glares at and rebukes Rabbi Elazar: an incident with conflict and an emotional reaction.

Rabbi Elazar teaches without attribution, Rabbi Yohanan grows angry, colleagues try to appease him and fail, Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi succeeds; a full narrative with conflict and resolution. The Gemara's explanation at the end of [6] is commentary.
A legal objection and dialectic about exemption from Shema; no event is narrated.
At Rabbi's funeral a launderer who missed it throws himself from a roof and dies, and a Divine Voice responds; clear events with consequence.
After the habitual frame of Hillel providing a horse and servant, a one-time event follows: he could not find a servant and ran before the man himself for three mil.
Rav Nahman's arrival frames a purely legal question-and-answer exchange with no conflict or event beyond speech.
Rabba reports finding Sages discussing a legal point and his reply; speech only, legal discussion, no conflict or event.
A report of Rav Huna's habitual practice cited as evidence; no one-time event follows.
Rav Ashi feeds Mar Zutra from the king's dish, is confronted, points out the leprous defect, which is found; actions, conflict and resolution.
A bandit led to execution confesses to killing Shimon the Priest and the wife is remarried on that basis; a narrated incident with a court response, followed by Rabbi Yehuda's reinterpretation.
Rav Amram, tempted by a captive woman, climbs a ladder, stops himself and cries fire, confronts the Sages and expels his evil inclination; a full narrative.
Rav Hamnuna is sent to Rav Huna, who sees his uncovered head, learns he is unmarried, turns his face away and banishes him until he marries; action and conflict.
A chain of legal objections and analogies; no event narrated.
A report of the song sung at an ordination, cited for its content; nothing follows and there is no conflict.
Ravina, holding an orphan's wine while taking his own to Sikhra, brings the case to Rav Ashi, who rules; an incident followed by a ruling.

A Mehoza woman and her Neharde'a husband come before Rav Nahman, who identifies her accent and rules, then reverses when challenged; an incident with a ruling. The closing question about Neharde'a's boundary is commentary.
A narrated wonder incident: a mustard branch breaks, yields nine kav, and its wood roofs a booth; R-C5 leaves such eyewitness wonders open, and the expert has accepted this kind on this page.
A man conditions a divorce on arriving in thirty days, is blocked by the ferry, calls out, and Shmuel rules; an incident followed by a ruling.
Only an ongoing avoidance by Rabbi Zeira is reported, as a lead-in to Rav Yehuda's dictum; no event follows within the passage.
A family whose children die young consults Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, follows his advice, and lives; events with change.
The dying Mar Ukva reviews his charity records, judges them insufficient and gives away half his wealth; a one-time event with change. The halakhic question that follows is commentary.
The Sages enter and leave by separate doors, Rabbi Akiva meets Yonatan ben Harkinas, withstands his objections and is rebuked; actions and conflict.
A man testifies before Rabbi Ami, is questioned, and Rabbi Ami elevates the other man to the priesthood; an incident followed by a ruling and action.

A witness recounts the lion-hearted traveler's deeds and death, Rabbi Tarfon cross-examines him and permits the wife to remarry; a narrated incident with a court response. The Gemara's opening question and closing remark are commentary.
A debtor sells two plots, the creditor seizes one and comes for the other, and the purchaser offers a hundred dinars; a concrete incident with conflict, resolved by a ruling in the following segment.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya finds a wise child in a Roman prison, swears to ransom him, does so, and the child becomes Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha; a full narrative.
Levi expounds, is not praised, re-expounds and is praised: only speech acts (expounding, praising), with mild tension and a change in outcome, so borderline at most.
A brother arrives and claims a share, is denied, comes before Rav Hisda, who rules on the burden of proof against a violent man: an incident with conflict and a ruling.
A one-time incident: a yevama comes to perform halitza before Rabbi Tarfon, and he responds by instructing those present. Thin, but something happens and a rabbi responds.
Rav Huna finds the Sages sitting and talking and argues with them; it is a halakhic discussion with no event beyond the speech, like the Yevamot 17a seating.
Habitual frame followed by a one-time event: Rav Rehumi stays away, his wife weeps, the roof collapses and he dies.
An exchange between Rabbi and his son, all speech, with a challenge and a rebuke ('be silent'): conflict without action, so borderline.
Something happens and people respond: two rabbis sitting, Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passes, they stand, and he reacts and rebukes them; actions plus a response, not a bare report.
A woman rebels, Mar Zutra compels her, and R. Hanina of Sura is born of the couple: an incident, a ruling and an outcome. The Gemara's 'that is not so' is commentary.
Eyewitness wonders (walking ankle-deep in fig honey; 'I myself saw'), the Ketubot 111b shape the expert accepted in review, though the edge is open.
R. Elazar sees a field and remarks on it. A dictum attached to a sighting, with no conflict and nothing following.
The Sages award Nakdimon's daughter a perfume allowance, she responds with a pointed blessing, and they answer amen: an incident with a ruling and a reaction.
The Sages seek to permit the Gibeonites and Rabbi objects; all speech, with disagreement but no action, so borderline.
A full story about Nebuzaradan and Zechariah's blood, a biblical-era episode the expert ruled out of scope (Gittin 57b).
A certain man betroths with a myrtle mat, is challenged, changes the betrothal object, the woman takes it silently, and Rava rules: incident plus ruling.
The rabbis' gathering frames embedded incidents: the captive couple who never touched and her eulogy, and the grain price falling until sinners were stoned.
R. Yehuda bars R. Meir's students, Sumakhos pushes his way in and teaches, R. Yehuda grows angry, and R. Yosei responds: actions, emotion and conflict.
A yevama falls to a man, his brother tries to disqualify her with a divorce, and they negotiate the property: a real incident with conflict, though mostly dialogue.
Customs of Judea and the Galilee with no one-time event following.
A Jew and a gentile walk together, the gentile reminds him of the Temple to slow him, he groans but keeps pace, and they exchange words: actions with a response.
The residents of Bei Harmakh divert a river, the upstream owners complain to Abaye, and he rules: incident plus ruling.
Rav Yehuda's summons before Rav Nahman, the Hasmonean litigant, Rav Mattana's arrival, the proclamation, torn marriage contracts and the attempted stoning: a full narrative.
Rabba bar bar Hana's eyewitness account of an Arab cutting open his camel, which died at once: a one-line eyewitness wonder of the kind the expert accepted, though the edge is open.
At his son's wedding Rava pours drinks; some rabbis stand, others do not, and he becomes angry and rebukes them: action, emotion and conflict.
A man passes Ravina bareheaded, Ravina reacts, and R. Yirmeya answers him: a small incident with a response, close to the borderline.
A mill owner grows rich and demands money instead of grinding, and the renter refuses: an incident with conflict. Ravina and Rav Avira's analysis afterwards is legal discussion, not story.
Two narrated incidents (a man riding on Shabbat, a man with his wife under a fig tree), each brought to court and punished; events plus a court's response.
Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai meets Nakdimon's impoverished daughter; actions, dialogue, recognition and his weeping form a full narrative about post-biblical figures.
Four hundred captive children ask, are answered, and leap into the sea; a full post-biblical narrative with action and consequence.
A woman obligated to an oath in Rav Beivai's court, litigants' requests, his ruling and Rav Pappi's rebuke: an incident followed by a ruling and reaction.
Rav Aha visits Rav Hisda and places his granddaughter on his lap, provoking a conflictual exchange; there is an action beyond speech and a response.
Mostly a halakhic exchange; the only events are finding them, falling silent and going to Rabba, but there is conflict (an unanswered challenge, Rabba's rebuke).
A man brings R. Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing; he refuses it, recuses himself, appoints judges and reflects on bribery: actions with consequence.
Rav Hisda's slave escapes and an exchange with the Samaritans follows; an event with conflict. Segment 3 is the Gemara's commentary and excluded.
A woman holding deposited documents is claimed against by heirs and Rav Nahman rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
Yehuda son of R. Hiyya is delayed one day, R. Yannai declares him dead, and he dies: a one-time event after a habitual frame, with consequence.
The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin buy a maidservant, the price rises, they come before R. Ami who rules: incident plus ruling.
A hypothetical legal case ('if one's bread was baked... and the father died'), not a narrated event.
Pure legal analysis of a mishna's reasoning; no narrated event.
R. Yohanan's relatives come to him about their stepmother's medical costs, he advises them, then regrets it: incident, ruling and reaction.
Judges rule, Reish Lakish reverses their decision, R. Yohanan criticizes him: a series of actions with conflict.
A brewer betroths with beer sediment, the owner finds him and comments, and Rava rules: incident plus ruling.
A man takes a Torah scroll from the synagogue and gives it to his wife as a divorce, and Rav Yosef rules: incident plus ruling.
R. Zeira reports finding R. Asi teaching a ruling; a transmission frame with no event beyond reporting a statement.
A woman seizes a silver cup and demands sustenance; she comes before Rava who rules: incident plus ruling.
A man picking dates is asked by a woman, proposes betrothal, she answers, and Rav Zevid rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
A man rents out a millstone, becomes rich, buys his own, and a dispute arises with the renter: a narrated incident with change and conflict.
A husband travels to collect his wife's inheritance, spends money, comes before R. Ami who rules and is challenged: incident plus ruling.
During a drought in Nehardea everyone sold their mansions, then wheat arrived, and Rav Nahman ruled: incident plus ruling.
The incident is only alluded to ('Rabbi gave her one-twelfth') as evidence in a legal argument; not enough of it is given.
An exchange of halakhic letters between Yohanan ben Bag Bag and R. Yehuda ben Beteira; only speech acts, but with a rebuke and disagreement.
One-time incident: bar Kappara did not stand, Rabbi Shimon became angry, went to his father, and his father responded. Actions, an emotional reaction and conflict.
Full narrative of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tricking the Angel of Death and entering paradise. A rabbi is the protagonist, so it is in scope.
Brief incident: Rav Pappa served a cup, Rav Yitzhak did not stand, and Rav Pappa became angry. An action plus an emotional reaction, with conflict; the answer that follows is the Gemara's.
Narrative of Rav Yosef son of Rava leaving the study hall, his father coming out armed to meet him, and the quarrel that left both missing the meal. Several actions with conflict.
A frame (Ravina found him leaning on a door) for an unresolved halakhic dilemma. Nothing happens and nothing follows.
Rav Nahman arrives in Sura, is asked a legal question and answers it from a mishna. Speech only, with no conflict.
Two one-time incidents in which a bathhouse and a stair collapse and the rabbis pull their supporters up, followed by the Sages' question and Rabbi Yohanan's reply. Real events with a response.

Rabbi Yishmael's sharecropper brings the fruit early. Rabbi Yishmael refuses it, disqualifies himself, appoints judges and reflects on his own bias. A one-time event with a development and a resolution.
Incident followed by a ruling: a man deposited silk, the custodian died, the claimant came before Rabbi Abba, and he ruled.
Purely legal statements, a discussion and a baraita about a hypothetical case. No event that happened.
The incident is only alluded to, as the facts behind a ruling. Not enough of the incident is given to make a story.
Giddel bar Re'ilai pays the tax in advance, the owners return and claim the land, and the case comes before Rav Pappa, with a dispute over the ruling. An incident followed by a ruling.
Someone came before Rav Yosef, who ruled, and the rest is a legal exchange with Abaye. Almost none of the incident is given; it is a legal discussion.
Eyewitness reports of wonders, including Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai's one-time walk in ankle-deep fig honey. The expert accepted this kind of 'I myself saw' account from Ketubot 111b.
A man brings Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing. Rabbi Yishmael refuses it, disqualifies himself, appoints judges and reflects on bribery. A one-time incident with a response.
A certain man betrothed a girl with a bundle of vegetables in the market, and Ravina ruled. Incident plus ruling, the shape of the cow case.
A rumor circulated about a woman's betrothal. Rav Hama summoned her father, heard his account and ruled. An incident followed by a ruling.
A man comes before Reish Lakish to testify about someone's priestly status, and what follows is questions and Rabbi Elazar's challenge. Mostly speech, with some conflict.
An incident in Shihin: a mustard branch broke, nine kav were found on it, and its wood roofed a booth, followed by a further report of a wonder. Things happened and people acted on them.
A bare report that Levi recited five blessings and Rav Asi six, cited as evidence of practice. Nothing follows.
After Rabbi Eliezer's death four elders refute him and Rabbi Yehoshua rebukes them. Almost entirely speech, but with conflict and an implied change.
Ravina's way of collecting the dowry is cited only as legal precedent. It is a report of what he did, with no narrative.
A habitual practice, 'when they would come before Rav Hisda he would say', with no one-time event, followed by Gemara discussion.
An incident is only alluded to ('I was involved in an incident, and they said') as the source of a ruling. Not enough of the incident is given.
A one-line allusion to an incident, cited as evidence for a halakha, with no development or response.
Ze'eiri avoids R. Yohanan's marriage offer; one day he carries him across a puddle and R. Yohanan confronts him. Actions, conflict and a one-time event.
Me'oret's slave dying is only alluded to as an objection in a legal discussion; not enough of the incident is given.
Rav Nahman's relative sells her ketuba, dies; buyers claim from the daughter; Rav Nahman advises, she forgives, and he later regrets it. Incident, response and change.
A certain man willed a palm tree to his daughter, the orphans withheld it, and Rav Yosef and Abaye ruled. Incident followed by a ruling.
Rabbi Yirmeya dozes while two sages discuss, wakes up and rebukes them as 'children'. Beyond speech there is the dozing and waking, plus conflict.
Abaye's boast and a sage's challenge to it are pure dialogue on exegesis; the challenge gives conflict but there is no action.
The passage only says Rami bar Hama's sister was married to Rav Avya; on its own no incident is given.
A woman obligated to swear in Rav Beivai's court, the litigant's demand, her counter-demand, and his ruling: an incident followed by a ruling.
A man helps Shmuel off a ferry, and Shmuel responds by disqualifying himself from the man's case. An act with a response.
Terminological and legal discussion with no narrated event.

In segment 4 people called a man 'son of the Aramean woman', casting doubt on his lineage, and Rav Asi ruled (and likewise R. Yehoshua ben Levi). Something happened to someone and a rabbi responded. Segments 2-3 are legal reasoning.
Mar Zutra visits the dying convert Rabbi Yehuda and acquires his slave; one departs to death, the other to life. Segment 4 is the Gemara's legal commentary.
R. Yohanan's relatives seize an orphans' cow and go back and forth between R. Yohanan and Reish Lakish. Incident, rulings and conflict.
A legal query about a bill of divorce is sent and answered; this is only quasi-speech (sending a question), with no event or conflict.
Rav Ami's permission, the Sages' objection and his reply are mostly speech acts with some conflict: the Ketubot 7a borderline shape.
Testimony cases come before Reish Lakish and R. Yohanan, and Reish Lakish looks harshly at R. Elazar and rebukes him: incident, response and conflict.
Rav Nahman bar Ya'akov passes in a gilt carriage; Rava goes to him while Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak first declines, then goes; he bares his arm and remarks on the wind. Actions and a one-time event.
An exegetical derivation of the dates of Moses' death and birth, not a narrated story.
Analytical discussion of why Abaye and Rava chose different sources; no event.
A hypothetical legal case about a general coming to a city, not an event that happened.
Marta bat Baitos brings King Yannai a measure of dinars until he appoints Yehoshua ben Gamla High Priest: a post-biblical event with action and consequence.
A creditor seizes an orphans' ox from a herdsman, the parties dispute, and Rav Nahman rules. Incident followed by a ruling.

A historical narrative: men would not marry, successive enactments failed, husbands kept dismissing their wives, until Shimon ben Shatah came and instituted the lien. A past custom followed by a one-time event and its resolution.
Peleimu's habitual taunt is followed by a one-time event: Satan comes as a pauper on the eve of Yom Kippur and is brought in and seated at the table. Action and conflict.
The passage is only the opening clause 'a certain man who was selling'; on its own no incident is given.
A halakhic query sent and an answer relayed; Rav Huna's death is incidental. Quasi-speech acts with no conflict.
Homa before Rava, her arm uncovered, Rava goes home, his wife drives Homa out of Mehoza: a chain of events with conflict and consequence.
The rabbis only intended to rule and were rebuked. Speech only, but with conflict.
A legal dilemma, a search of sources and a ruling sent out. No incident is narrated.
Rabbi Akiva sees Rabbi Meir's boat sink, then meets him alive and hears how the waves saved him: a narrated personal incident.
A gift to Rav Anan, his referral to Rav Nahman, Rav Nahman's mistaken deference and the other litigant losing: a causal chain of events.
Mishna and legal-exegetical discussion. The Rebecca verse is used only as a prooftext.
An incident (a maidservant immerses and a bone is found in her teeth) followed by Rabbi's ruling to immerse again: incident plus ruling.
A man sells rights, his mother dies, he contests the sale, and the rabbis rule: a narrated incident resolved by a ruling.
Pure legal argument built on hypothetical cases.
Hananya ben Hakhinai's twelve-year absence, his return, his wife's death and her revival: a full narrative.
A virginity dispute brought to Rabban Gamliel, who runs a test with maidservants and then the bride and rules: actions and resolution.
Court incidents: Rava reverses an oath on his wife's word, then rejects Rav Pappa's lone testimony and is challenged. Incidents plus rulings.
A certain man selling beads tries to betroth a woman who says 'give, give', and Rav Hama rules: the incident-plus-ruling shape.
A man betroths with a bundle of rags and Rav Shimi examines it to rule: a brief incident plus ruling, followed by Gemara discussion.
After the Roman custom comes a one-time event (the two captive children's exchange), then Beitar's schoolchildren resist and are burned. Post-biblical events.
A bequest of a palm tree, the orphans ignore it, Rav Yosef and Abaye rule: incident plus ruling.
Embedded in the letter is an incident: a lovesick man meant to leave the Land, heard the teaching, and suffered there until he died. The rest of the letter is advice.
The incident before Rabbi Yitzhak is only alluded to. The passage is his legal statement.
A claimed brother arrives and demands a share, is refused, goes to Rav Hisda, and the burden of proof is shifted onto the violent man: conflict and resolution.
Brief incidents: a man does a judge a small favour and the judge disqualifies himself. Action plus response.
Debtor dies, creditor repossesses, orphans pay, he repossesses again, Abaye rules: incident plus ruling.
A pauper eats lentils with Rabbi Nehemya and dies, and Nehemya laments: events with consequence. The Gemara's gloss follows.

A sequence of events: Rav Sheshet sends Rav Yosef for money, the merchants ask for an acquisition, he agrees then evades them, and Rav Sheshet responds on his return; multiple actions with a resolution.
Someone merely comes to ask, and the rest is a legal exchange between Rav Yosef and Abaye. Not enough of an incident is given.
The brothers divided their property and came before Rav Ashi, who ruled: an incident followed by a ruling.
Rabbi Hanina declines the appointment and sits outside, Levi joins him, Afes dies, Levi goes to Babylonia, and Rav works out what happened: a chain of events.
His relatives came to Rabbi Yohanan, he advised them, and later he regretted it: an incident with a response and a consequence. The opening statement in segment 2 is a lead-in.
The Aramaic only alludes to 'that incident' with a certain woman; the narrative comes from the translator. The incident is alluded to, not told.
The orphans used the widow's robe as a shroud and Rava ruled: an incident followed by a ruling.
A man betrothed with a stone, Rav Hisda estimated its value, the mother objected and Rav Hisda answered: an incident with a ruling and a dispute.
Levi's request and the rabbis' practice of supplying each other are reported as evidence for a halakhic position. Nothing happens and nothing follows.
The people of Bei Mikhsi were seized for debt and came before Rav Huna, who ruled, and Rabbi Abba challenged him: an incident with a ruling and a dispute.
A man states where he is from and Rabbi Yitzhak declares where that place is, followed by halakhic discussion. It is speech with no conflict and no event.
The husband gave one of the first wife's maidservants to his second wife; she cried out before Rava, who ignored her: an incident and a response.
Two incidents: the bathhouse and the stair collapse and the rabbis pull their supporters up, followed by an exchange with the Sages.
The agent paid the debt, the creditors refused to return the document, and the case came before Rabbi Abbahu, who ruled: an incident followed by a ruling.
A habitual frame (Rabbi Tarfon's service to his mother) is followed by a one-time event: he boasts in the study hall and is rebuked.
A disputed field: the steward argues before Abaye in stages, wins, and Abaye praises him. An incident with rulings and a resolution.
Ameimar's permission to marry draws a challenge from Rav Ashi, which he rejects. It is mostly halakhic speech, but there is conflict.
A yevama refuses levirate marriage; Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba tricks the yavam into halitza and then gets a proper one. Actions with conflict and a resolution.
Rav Yehuda forces a get three times while the husband keeps voiding it, and has the witnesses stop their ears: a sequence of actions with conflict, cited as proof.
A man sold his property to move to Eretz Yisrael, went, failed to settle, and Rava ruled: an incident followed by a ruling.
Rabbi Elazar's objection silences Rabbi Yohanan, who praises him, learns from Reish Lakish that it is a baraita, and goes and masters Torat Kohanim: events and a change.
The Sages award Nakdimon's daughter a perfume allowance; she answers them pointedly and they say Amen. An incident with a ruling and a response.
The mikveh at Yavne is found deficient, Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva dispute its purifications, and Tarfon concedes with praise: an incident, rulings, conflict and a resolution.
Rabbi Zeira crosses the Jordan on a rope, a Sadducee mocks him, and he answers: an action with conflict and a response.
A bare report that two sages each elevated someone on a relative's word. Nothing follows.
Rami bar Yehezkel visits Benei Berak, sees milk and honey mixing, and comments: a one-time eyewitness wonder, the kind the expert accepted at Ketubot 111b.
A goblet deposited with Hasa, who dies leaving no instructions, and the case comes before Rav Nahman, who rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
A halakhic question and answer reported by an earwitness; speech only, no conflict and no event beyond the exchange.
Rav Aha's habitual dancing with the bride is a practice; the only follow-up is the Sages' question and his answer, so there is little beyond a custom and a dialogue.
A certain man drinking in a shop, a woman's request, his attempted betrothal and her reply, resolved by Rav Hama's ruling: an incident followed by a ruling.
Purely legal argumentation about konamot and liens; no narrated event.
King Agrippa (post-biblical) yielded to a bride's procession and the Sages praised him: an event with a response.
Abaye's tenant asks, Abaye rules, Rav Yosef corrects him, Abaye runs after the tenant and fails to catch him, then draws the lesson: a full narrative with actions and consequence.
A divorced betrothed couple came before Rava, who placed an intermediary between them, challenged by Rav Adda bar Mattana: an incident with a court's action, given in two versions.
The passage opens the quoted incident of Rabban Gamliel and the Elders traveling on a ship and his transfer of tithes, a Talmudic citation of a narrated event.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna seize the boat, are challenged by Rav Pinehas bar Ami, and Rava rebukes and rules against them: actions, conflict and resolution.
The blind man late to Mar Shmuel, the messenger who reports adultery, and Mar Shmuel's ruling form a narrated incident; segment 3 is the Gemara's commentary on it and is excluded.
A man bequeathed a palm tree to his daughter, the orphans divided the estate without giving it, and Rav Yosef and Abaye ruled: an incident followed by a ruling.
Opening of the Yeimar bar Hashu boat incident: the agent seizes the boat and is confronted by Rav Pappa and Rav Huna; narrated actions with conflict.

Continuation of Reish Lakish's consolation visit: he repeatedly commands his disseminator, who stands and delivers blessings, as part of a narrated event; Abaye's comment in segment 4 is commentary and excluded.
Two incidents: Mar bar Rav Ashi physically treated a man and declared him fit; in Pumbedita Rav Beivai thought to permit a case and Rav Pappi rebuked him and ruled otherwise.
Two deeds came before Rav Yosef, he awarded the field, and the losing claimant protested and petitioned him: an incident with ruling and conflict.
Abaye accuses Rav Ika bar Avin of self-interest over a yevama, Rav Ika retorts, and they go and ask Rav Hananel: conflict plus action beyond speech.
Generic reports of how Rav Yehuda and Rava responded when such persons came before them, cited as evidence of their view; no specific incident unfolds.
Halakhic conclusion with a passing allusion to a woman who strangled her child, cited and dismissed as evidence; not enough of the incident is given.
A woman came before Rav Nahman seeking divorce, argued with him, and he ruled to force the husband: an incident followed by a ruling.
Rav Hiyya Arikha's widowed mother-in-law sues him, Rabba bar Sheila rules and writes an authorization, he defies it and appeals to Rava, and she argues with Rava: a sustained narrative of litigation.
Queen Helene's vow during her son's war, her immigration, and Beit Hillel's ruling, quoted by the Talmud from the Mishnah: incident plus ruling about a post-biblical figure.
The passage holds the resolution of the incident (Rabbi Yonatan forced the sons to feed their father, hence the man kissed his foot); the remainder is Gemara commentary and not part of the story.
Continuation of the Marta bat Baitos narrative during the siege: her death, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's response, and her throwing her gold into the market.
A scholarly exchange: Rav Dimi reports a ruling, Abaye challenges him, Rav Dimi falls silent, Abaye resolves it and is praised; essentially speech, but with conflict and implied change.
A man passes before Ravina without covering his head, Ravina reacts, and Rabbi Yirmeya responds: something happens and people respond, though the episode is minimal.
A baraita's hypothetical rulings and the Gemara's legal analysis; no event that happened is narrated.
An agent pays a debt, is refused the document, and the case comes before Rabbi Abbahu who rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
Reports of Rabbi Yohanan's and Rava's habitual practice cited as evidence for the halakha, with no one-time event following.
A bare report of Rav Zevid's ruling or practice, with nothing following.
Abaye rules for his tenant, is corrected by Rav Yosef, and runs parasangs after the tenant without catching him: events, conflict and consequence.
The widow, the baked dinar, her oath and her child's death form a full incident. Segment 4 is the Gemara's commentary on it.
Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebels holding a garment, the Sages rule, and Rav Gamda rebukes them for flattery: an incident with a ruling and conflict.
Almost entirely speech reporting a study-hall debate, but there is conflict (Reish Lakish screaming and being ignored).
Brief reports of Rav Kahana taking a cloth and Mar bar Rav Ashi buying one, cited as precedents, with no continuation.
The dying master throws his hat to the crying maidservant and Rav Nahman rules, framed by the inquiry about what happened. Segment 5 is the Gemara's commentary.
A certain man sets a conditional divorce, is stranded by the ferry and calls out, and Shmuel rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
Geneiva passes by, the rabbis argue over whether to rise, he approaches and greets them, and they exchange words and an invitation to eat. There is action and conflict beyond speech.
A maidservant is captured and redeemed by a gentile as a wife, and the Sages send Rabbi Abba bar Zutra instructions: something happens and others respond.
Abba bar Marta disguises himself with wax and passes his creditors unrecognized: actions with a goal and an outcome.
A one-line report that Rava coerced Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity, cited as a precedent with no continuation.
Ravin goes to betroth a woman for his son but betroths her himself, and the Gemara probes his motives: an incident with a turn.
The relatives consult Rabbi Yohanan, then Reish Lakish, who threatens them, and Rabbi Yohanan concedes: a sequence of events with conflict.
Captives are redeemed, one is pregnant by a gentile, and Rabbi Ami rules. Segments 3-4 are Rav Yosef's legal response, not part of the incident.
The Gemara quotes the Mishnah's incident of the divorce bill brought before Rabban Gamliel, which he validated. The Talmud's citation of a Mishnah story can be included.
A certain scribe comes before Rabbi Abbahu confessing a defect, and Rabbi Abbahu rules: an incident followed by a ruling, in the 'a certain man' shape.
A yevama falls to a man, his brother tries to disqualify her by a get, and they negotiate over the property: an incident with conflict.
Legal argument; the strangling incident in segment 4 is only alluded to in one clause and dismissed.
Only an introductory fragment ('a certain person said to them'); the incident's content lies outside the passage.
The Sages switch the names of the disputants and send the question to Rav, who reacts with an oath: action beyond speech, with conflict.
The host and Rav Beivai quarrel over an appointment, Rav Yosef rules, and Rav Adda bar Ahava's argument wins his host the post: an incident with a ruling.
Rabba reports finding scholars discussing a halakhic dispute and his reply; pure scholarly speech with no event beyond speaking and no conflict that leads anywhere.
A certain woman came before Rabbi Ami demanding her ketubah; after an exchange he rules that the husband is forced to divorce her. An incident followed by a ruling, with conflict.
A certain man willed a palm tree to his daughter, died and left two half-trees; a narrated incident (the ruling that resolves it follows in the next segment).
An interpretive exchange about a mishna (needle, pearl) between scholars; Rav Yosef's rebuke is part of academic argument, with no narrated event.
A man wills a palm tree to his daughter and dies leaving two halves; the heirs' dispute is brought to Rav Ashi and resolved by a cited ruling. Incident plus ruling.
Rabba 'performed an action' on a found bill of divorce; the incident is only alluded to and the passage is a dispute about its circumstances, not enough of the incident is given.
A report of what Rav Kahana did with an orphan's beer and his rationale, cited as evidence of practice; nothing follows from it.
At his son's wedding Rav Pappa poured a cup for Rav Yitzhak, who did not stand, and Rav Pappa became angry: action, slight, emotional response.
Two incidents: a man removes a feather from Ameimar's head / covers spittle before Mar Ukva, then reveals he has a case, and the judge disqualifies himself. Action and consequence.
A man whose betrothed died comes before the seated rabbis, who rule, and Rav Hiyya objects with a baraita; incident plus ruling. Segment 3 is Gemara inference and commentary.
A man deposited pearls with Rabbi Meyasha, who died without instructions; the parties came before Rabbi Ami who ruled for the depositor. Incident followed by ruling.
The judges report that Rav Yehuda acted in a case of branches; the incident is only alluded to and cited as evidence of his view.
The captive son and daughter of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha are paired by their masters, weep all night, recognize each other at dawn and die. A full story.
During a famine the Sages ask Rav Yosef to pray and he refuses with an argument; beyond the background situation the exchange is speech, with some tension but no action following.
A halakhic dialogue between Rav Hisda and Rav Yosef about a betrothed orphan's sustenance, with an alternate version; speech only, no event.
A man in a synagogue appoints two of three present to write his get, then the schoolteacher dies; the case is disputed and Rava rules. Incident plus ruling.
A baraita's general legal procedure for a death before a wedding and its qualification; hypothetical law, not an event that happened.
Aher sees the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator dragged by a pig, exclaims, and goes out and sins: an event, reaction and consequence about a post-biblical figure.
A debtor sells two plots; the creditor repossesses one and comes for the other; the purchaser takes 100 zuz to him with an offer. A narrated incident with action and response.

After an amoraic dispute the question is sent to Rav with the names reversed and Rav swears in reply; quasi-speech acts (sending a question) with conflict, but no event beyond speech. Segment 2 is a legal dispute only.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seize an orphans' cow; Rabbi Yohanan approves, Reish Lakish orders it returned, and Yohanan concedes. Incident, conflicting rulings, outcome.
Ulla slights Rav Hamnuna's lineage, Rav Hamnuna is ashamed, and Ulla resolves it by questioning him about his poll tax; an emotional reaction (an event) with conflict and resolution.
Ravnai, visiting to sell sesame, transmits a ruling; Ameimar praises it and Rav Ashi jibes at him. Essentially speech with some conflict, no further action.
Rabban Gamliel sees Rabbi Akiva's ship sink, grieves, then meets him alive and asks how he survived; a first-person narrative of events and reactions, concluding with his remark.
A man snatches a belt from a woman seller and offers it back as betrothal; she takes it in silence, and Rav Nahman rules. Incident followed by a ruling.

A man comes before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi with a virginity claim, the bride disputes, the cloth is brought and washed, blood is found, and he rules; a narrated incident with conflict, actions and a ruling.
A specific man comes before R. Yehoshua ben Levi, is questioned, and someone is elevated to Levite status: an incident followed by a ruling and an action.
A certain man sells his mother's ketubah, she dies, he contests the sale, and Rami bar Hama and Rava rule: a narrated incident resolved by a ruling.
Two 'a certain man... a woman came' incidents of attempted betrothal, each followed by Rav Hama's ruling; narrated events with a resolution, though thin and mostly speech.
A man snatches a belt from a woman selling belts, proposes betrothal, she takes it silently, and Rav Nahman rules: incident plus ruling.
A Mishnah legal case stated hypothetically (one who marries a woman...) with a dispute of tannaim; no event that happened.
An account of how a ruling was transmitted and its attribution corrected; speech and quasi-speech (sent, said) with no real conflict or event beyond it.
Rav Ashi's slave Minyamin is immersed: handed over, bridled, loosened and tightened, given a clay bucket and sent home. Segments 4-5 are a separate halakhic question and answer.
At the wedding of Rabban Gamliel's son he serves drinks, R. Eliezer refuses, R. Yehoshua accepts, and a dispute follows; the Abraham exemplum is cited inside a rabbinic story, so it is in scope.
R. Elazar recites Rav's ruling before Shmuel, who mocks him ('feed Elazar barley'), and R. Zeira later recalls it; speech acts only, but with conflict.
The bar Tzartzur heirs come before Rav Amram, ignore his advice, are threatened with excommunication and sent to Rav Nahman, who rules: a dispute with actions and a resolution.
Rav Hiyya bar Adda misses three days of teaching to harvest a miraculous vine and Reish Lakish rebukes him: events, conflict and a consequence.
Rav Yitzhak bar Bisna loses the study-hall keys on Shabbat and comes to R. Pedat, who tells him to have children walk there: incident plus ruling. The Gemara's inference in segment 3 is commentary.
'An incident came before R. Yitzhak in Antioch' only alludes to an incident; none of it is given, only the ruling.
A certain man sells his property to go up to Eretz Yisrael, goes but cannot settle, and Rava rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
A Mishnah story: a girl drawing water is raped and R. Yohanan ben Nuri rules on her marrying a priest. Incident plus ruling, but by R-C1 it belongs to the Mishnah, not the Talmud.

Shmuel's father guards captive women; Shmuel's own daughters are later taken captive, outwit their captors in R. Hanina's court and are permitted, and R. Hanina tells Rav Shemen to marry one: a full narrative.
A hypothetical legal scenario about witnesses and a priest's status, constructed by the Gemara; no event that happened.
Embedded in Rav Ulla's answer: the Sages seek a deal with Dama ben Netina, who gives up a fortune rather than wake his father. A post-biblical figure, so in scope.
Rav Pappa goes to write his son's ketubah, Yehuda bar Mareimar comes out to meet him and takes his leave at the door: narrated actions that open a story.

Rav Yosef son of Rava's widow comes before Rav Nehemya and asks for food and wine, which he grants on the custom of Mehoza: an incident before a judge resolved by a ruling, though thin and mostly speech.
Dying, Mar Ukva reviews his charity records, judges them insufficient and gives away half his wealth. The Gemara's question about the one-fifth limit is commentary (R-B4).
Mar Zutra visits the dying convert R. Yehuda from India and has the convert's slave carry his shoes in order to acquire him: events with a consequence.
A man brings Rav Anan a gift, Rav Anan disqualifies himself, then accepts it and sends the man to Rav Nahman, who misreads the letter: a narrative of actions and consequences.
R. Zeira, finding no ferry, crosses the Jordan on a rope, a Sadducee mocks him and he answers: an action plus conflict and a response.
The incident of Beloreya, whose slaves immersed before her, came before the Sages and they ruled. That is an event followed by a ruling, cited inside an objection.
Letters are sent, Rav Sheshet is dispatched under threat of excommunication, and Rav Anan goes to Mar Ukva. There are actions beyond speech, and a conflict that escalates.
The parents quarrel and the father is pressured into agreeing. During the meal the father's relative climbs onto the roof and betroths the girl. A one-time sequence of events with a conflict.

Shmuel's father guards the captives and rebukes Shmuel. Shmuel's daughters are later captured, outwit the court and are recognized, and Rabbi Hanina tells Rav Shemen to marry one. A full narrative with a reversal.
A custom adopted in a time of danger, followed by halakhic rules. No one-time event follows the custom.
A woman obligated to take an oath, a litigant's demand and her counter-demand, the court's ruling, and Rav Pappi's rebuke of the judge. An incident with a ruling and a reaction.
A mother writes conflicting deeds to two sons, two judges rule in opposite directions, and the judges confront each other. An incident, its rulings and a conflict.
A teacher is absent for three days and explains it by a miraculous harvest. Reish Lakish rebukes him. A one-time event with a response.

Cases in Neharde'a and Pumbedita were decided and the money collected, and Rav Nahman threatens to seize the judges' houses unless they reverse. Thin on the incident itself, but there are events and a conflict.
Rav Hisda tells Rabba to look into a ruling, and he does. The 'event' is only a frame for halakhic analysis: no conflict, nothing follows.
A question put to Rabbi Eliezer and his answer. Speech only, with no conflict, followed by Gemara analysis.
A creditor repossesses land, the orphans redeem it, he seizes it again, and they come before Abaye, who rules. An incident followed by a ruling.
The Gemara's commentary on the Mishnah's innkeeper story, explaining why she was believed. This is commentary, not the story.
Three sisters' sons die after circumcision, and the fourth sister comes before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who rules. Events followed by a ruling.
Rav Kahana's single act of accepting a cloth, cited as precedent for a legal point. No one responds and nothing follows.
An agent cannot find the intermediary, three Sages devise a solution, Rav Safra objects, and they are embarrassed. Rava's and Rav Ashi's evaluations in [4]-[5] are commentary.
Rav Huna's habitual practice when cases came before him, cited as an example. A custom with no one-time event.
Conflicting attributions of rulings and halakhic analysis. Nothing is narrated.
A one-line allusion to where the Mishnah's incident took place, used for legal reasoning. Not enough of the incident is given.
A habitual frame, then one day Rav Rehumi stays at study, his wife weeps, and the roof collapses under him. A one-time event follows the custom.
A habitual frame, then one day Rav Rehumi stays at study, his wife weeps, and the roof collapses under him. A one-time event follows the custom.
A man betrothed a woman with silk and Rabba and Rav Yosef ruled on it: an incident with rulings. Segment [3] is legal analysis.
Rabbi Hama bar Bisa comes home after twelve years, fails to recognize his son, is distressed, and stands before him, and his wife rebukes him. A full narrative.
Homa comes before Rava, her arm is exposed, Rava goes home, and his wife drives Homa out of Mehoza. A full narrative with conflict.
After a habitual note, a one-time event: rabbis fail to stand for Abaye, he challenges them, and they explain. An action (not standing) with a conflict.
Incidents came before the courts of Neharde'a and Pumbedita, they ruled, and Rav Nahman ordered them to reverse under threat; an incident followed by rulings and a response.
A one-line report of what Rava did, cited as precedent for a legal point, with no continuation.
The incident is only alluded to in support of Ulla's ruling; not enough of it is given to be a story.
Orphans came before Rava, he ruled, the Sages objected and he answered; an incident with a ruling and a response.
Rav Sheshet coerced a get, the man subverted it before witnesses, and Rav Sheshet required another; a narrated incident with consequence.
A bare report of the blessing Rav Haviva recited, followed only by a halakhic ruling against him; nothing follows the act.
Ben Yasiyan's first-person account of travelling overseas, finding a convert in a forbidden-seeming marriage, challenging him and being answered.
A widow comes before Rav Yosef, he apportions sustenance and wine, she demands silk and retorts to his challenge; actions with conflict.
Purchase, hiring sailors, the river dammed, a demand, and Rava's rebuke in court; a full incident with a ruling.
A woman comes before Rav Yosef with a claim that conflicts with the Sages' rule, is rebuked, and confesses; a confrontation that reveals narrated events.
Abaye's boast and a Sage's challenge are speech with some conflict but no action; what follows is a halakhic answer.
A man complains to Rabban Gamliel, the bride responds, he investigates her family and rules; incident, investigation and resolution.
Elders boycott the lecture, Rav Hamnuna is sent to ostracize them, is stumped and mocked, and reports back to Rav Hisda.
Orphans whose property was held by Rabbi Banai came before Shmuel, who ordered him to sustain them; an incident followed by a ruling.
A one-line report that Rav Shimi used a remedy and the patient was healed, cited as evidence for the remedy; no story develops.
A man sold land to Rav Pappa, no longer needed the money, and Rav Pappa returned it; an incident with a response.
After the habitual mockery, one day Satan appears as a woman, Rabbi Akiva climbs, and is released with a heavenly warning.
The incidents are only alluded to as precedents with contrary rulings; the rest is legal discussion about the rulings.
On his deathbed Rabbi calls his sons in turn and hands over wisdom and the office of Nasi; part of a narrative.
After Mar Ukva's habit, one day the pauper pursues them, they hide in a furnace, his legs are singed and his wife explains; a full story.
Vespasian's siege, the wealthy men's provisions, and the zealots burning the stores causing famine; post-biblical figures, so in scope.
Reish Lakish sells himself to gladiators, kills them by a ruse, returns home, and dies leaving little; a full narrative.
Judges ruled, Reish Lakish reversed their action, and Rabbi Yohanan criticized him; an incident with rulings and a response.
Ulla dies outside the Land, Rabbi Elazar laments, is told the coffin is coming, and responds; an event with reactions.
Rav takes leave of Rabbi Hiyya, receives a cryptic blessing, searches and finds its meaning, borne out by his wife's conduct.
Rav Yosef son of Rava leaves study to go home; his father takes a weapon and goes out to meet him, they quarrel, and both miss the pre-fast meal. Actions, conflict and a consequence.
Geneiva passes, the two rabbis disagree about standing for a quarrelsome man, he comes over and teaches. Almost all speech with some tension, little action beyond it.
A specific incident: a harvester is bitten by a snake and dies, his wife informs the court, they verify, and a ruling follows. Incident plus ruling.
A woman taken as collateral in Ashkelon, her family distances her, witnesses testify and the Sages rule. An event with responses and a resolution.

R. Elazar b. R. Yosei's first-person account of testifying once with the result that a slave was (nearly) elevated to priesthood: an event with a consequence. The Gemara's emendation in [3] is commentary revising the story.
Extended narrative: R. Yishmael b. R. Yosei steps over heads, clashes with Abdon, a yevama arrives, Abdon is humiliated and punished with leprosy and the loss of his sons.
A certain man bequeaths his property to Toviya, dies, Toviya comes, and R. Yohanan rules. Thin, but an incident followed by a ruling.
A groom complains before Rabbi; Rabbi sees their hunger, has them bathed and fed, the groom then finds blood, and Rabbi rules and quotes a verse. Several actions in causal sequence.
Medical lore Abaye quotes from his foster mother. General remedies, no event.
Eyewitness report: a woman comes before Ameimar with a claim, her brothers speak, and Ameimar stays silent. It is cited as evidence of his view. Speech only, with a dispute between the parties.
A woman holding deposited documents is sued by the heirs, they come before Rav Nahman, and he questions her and rules. Incident plus ruling.
The tumtum of Biri is only alluded to as a counterexample in a legal argument. The incident is not narrated.
Inside Rabbi's deathbed dicta is an embedded incident: the people of Bireta DeSatya catch fish on Shabbat, R. Ahai excommunicates them, and they become apostates. Actions and a consequence.
Bar Haddaya asks two authorities and gets two answers. A consultation, all quasi-speech, with no event and no conflict beyond differing rulings; [3] is legal reasoning.
A man assesses orphans' coral for himself, it rises in value, he comes before R. Ammi, who rules. Incident plus ruling.
An academic exchange: R. Abba teaches, R. Safra objects, and R. Abba reports a chain of questions up to Rav. Speech only, no real conflict.
A woman signs her property over to her daughter to keep it from her husband, then marries and divorces. These are the narrated events of an incident whose resolution follows.
The heirs claim the deposited documents from a woman, the case comes before Rav Nahman, and he rules. Incident plus ruling.
Rav sends a halakhic question in a letter, R. Hiyya asks for clarification, and Rabbi answers. Quasi-speech acts with no conflict.
The Sages award Nakdimon's daughter-in-law wine, she blesses them, and they decline to answer amen. An incident with a ruling and a pointed response.
Rav and Rav Yehuda walking behind a woman. Mostly a dialogue in which Rav's urging is challenged; there is tension and an implied change of pace but little narrated action.
Yehuda bar Mareimar is pressed into visiting, sits silent, Abba of Sura misreads it and writes over all his property, and they then talk it out. Actions, misunderstanding, resolution.
R. Hanina bar Pappi resists a noblewoman with magic boils, she heals him, he flees to a dangerous bathhouse and is protected. A full narrative.
Rav Huna tears silk in front of his son to test whether he will grow angry: a deliberate act aimed at a response. The Gemara's halakhic questions and added details are commentary.
A woman signs her property over to evade her husband, divorces, Rav Nahman tears the deed, Rav Anan complains to Mar Ukva, who backs the ruling. Incident, ruling and conflict.

After the custom of costly burials, Rabban Gamliel acts once (has himself buried in linen) and the whole people follow him, so something happens and the world changes. Rav Pappa's remark is an appended comment.
Abaye's tenant asks, Abaye rules, Rav Yosef corrects him, and Abaye runs three parasangs after the tenant and fails to catch him. That is a sequence of events with consequences.
Two short incidents: a man does a judge a small favour, and Ameimar and then Mar Ukva respond by disqualifying themselves. Something happens and a rabbi responds.
An institutional history of how the priestly court changed the widow's ketubah amount. It has no particular incident or person, and serves as a reconstruction of legislation.
Purely legal discussion of hypothetical cases. No event is narrated.
A particular woman owes an oath, Rav Hisda's daughter testifies that she is suspect, and Rava reverses the oath. An incident followed by a ruling.
A teaching exchange between Rav Yehuda and his son: speech only, with nothing happening beyond the remark, and the Gemara's harmonization follows.
Rabbi Simlai's remark to his host is speech only, with no conflict and no event. It is cited as legal evidence.
A certain man betroths with a myrtle mat, bystanders object, he changes his declaration, she takes it in silence, and Rava rules. An incident followed by a ruling.

Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa delays the Angel of Death, then argues with him. At his death a pillar of fire appears, and Rabbi Alexandri makes it depart. A full narrative; the Abaye and Rav Adda exchange is appended commentary.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak juggles myrtle at weddings and Rabbi Zeira objects. At his death a pillar of fire appears, and Rabbi Zeira reverses his judgment. Conflict, an event and a change.
Rav Avya's wife's ketubah is lost and the couple come before Rav Yosef. Abaye objects to his ruling, and Rav Yosef tells them to write a new one. An incident followed by a ruling.
After a habitual frame, a one-time event follows: Yehuda is delayed, Rabbi Yannai declares him dead, and he dies.
Embedded in the letter is an incident: a man lovesick for a woman wanted to leave the Land, heard this teaching and stayed, suffering until he died. The rest of the letter is advice.
Rav Yehuda's practice of struggling to read, followed by Ulla's advice: speech with no conflict and nothing following.
Legal dialectic that only alludes to the David and Bathsheba incident; no story is narrated.
Academic legal argument. Rav Hiyya bar Avin's recollection is part of the debate, not a narrated event.
A bare report that Rabbi was moved to Tzippori when he fell ill, cited to resolve a contradiction. Nothing follows from it.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov sends his son to study, then goes himself. Abaye denies him lodging, and he defeats the seven-headed demon. A full narrative.
A certain man is punctured by a thorn and later has children. Shmuel sends the case to Rav, who responds. An incident followed by a ruling.
A man helps Shmuel off the ferry, and Shmuel learns he has a case and disqualifies himself. Something happens and a rabbi responds.
Rabbi Evyatar meets Elijah and challenges him, and Elijah resolves the challenge. A post-biblical rabbi's encounter with Elijah is in scope; segment 2 is exegetical setup.
Ravina recites the blessing at the betrothal, confident the match will hold, and then the other family retracts. An event with a reversal. The Rav Tahlifa line is a bare report with a ruling.
A beautiful woman claims to be betrothed in order to deter suitors, later betroths herself, is questioned by the Sages and explains, and a ruling follows.
A widow is refused by Rabba bar Rav Huna and curses him. He overturns his chair, yet still falls ill. Conflict, actions and a consequence.

The Exilarch asks Rav Huna, who steps out; Rav Hisda answers in his absence, Rav Huna returns, finds them, and reacts with an oath and praise. These are actions beyond speech, and there is a social turn.
Something happened: Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law seized a saddlebag of coins, and the Sages tried but could not take it from her. An incident with a response from the court.

A full narrative: the Sages visit Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, are received, question him, then leave and Akiva meets Yonatan. Segment 12 is the Gemara's commentary on Haggai's rulings, so it is excluded.
A medical remedy, with a one-line report about a goat cited as corroboration. Nobody responds and nothing follows.
An incident: a man leaves a palm tree to his daughter, dies leaving two half-trees, and the heirs want to give her those. The dispute is then taken up by the rabbis.
Beyond the list of rabbis made impotent, Rav Aha bar Ya'akov falls ill, is suspended from the cedar column and healed, then reflects on it. Something happens to him and there is a response.
Rabba bar bar Hana loses a bill of divorce, offers a distinguishing mark and visual recognition, gets it back, and then reflects on why it was returned.
A legislative proposal, a report that hard times prevented the vote, and a rhetorical remark. This is a legal-historical discussion with no narrated incident someone responds to.
At his son's wedding Rava pours drinks, some rabbis stand and others do not, and Rava becomes angry and rebukes them. Actions, conflict and an emotional reaction.
The sharecropper is late, Rabbi Yannai tithes in advance, consults Rabbi Hiyya, and they discuss a dream. An incident followed by a ruling.
A widow comes before Rav Yosef and he awards her sustenance and wine; she then demands silk and gives a pointed answer. A case with a ruling, and some tension.
A man whose betrothed has died comes before the rabbis, they rule, and Rav Hiyya challenges the ruling. Segment 3 is analysis of the rule, not narrative.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tricks the Angel of Death, jumps into paradise, keeps the knife, and meets Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai. A full narrative.

A man sells his property to move to Eretz Yisrael but never goes, and Rav Ashi rules on the sale. This is the incident-plus-ruling shape of R-C0, although most of the segment analyses the two versions of the ruling.
Two incidents of physical strength: a bathhouse collapses under Rabbi Abbahu and a stair under Rabbi Yohanan. Each pulls his helpers up, and Rabbi Yohanan replies to the Sages.
Rabbi Yehoshua is asked a halakhic question and answers with a deflection and a testimony. Speech only, with no event and no real conflict between the people involved.
Rav Ilish is taken captive with Rav Nahman's daughters, receives the bird omens, overhears the daughters, escapes, and later judges them. A full narrative.
A man whose brother died abroad, leaving a widow due for levirate marriage, comes to Rabbi Hanina and is answered sharply. Something happened to someone and a rabbi responded.
The heirs of bar Tzartzur come before Rav Amram, refuse his advice, are threatened, and are sent on to Rav Nahman, who rules. Conflict, action and resolution.
Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law seizes a saddlebag of coins and the Sages cannot remove it from her. An incident with a response from the court.
Rav raises an objection, Shmuel's father falls silent, and Rav mocks him with a verse. Speech and silence with conflict but no event beyond speaking; the Gemara's follow-up question is commentary.
Two Rabbi Meir incidents. He stops a steward, ignores a dream that tells him otherwise; and he makes peace between two quarrelers, after which Satan laments.
The sons buy a maidservant and leave silver as collateral, her price rises, and they go before Rabbi Ami, who rules. An incident followed by a ruling.
A habitual frame (Avimi's custom of honouring his father) is followed by a one-time event: his father dozes off, Avimi stands over him until he wakes, and is rewarded.
A woman who has seized a silver cup demands sustenance, comes before Rava, and he orders the orphans to pay. An incident followed by a ruling.
An incident before R. Yohanan (two sons die after circumcision, he rules for the third), followed by Abaye relying on it, marrying Huma and dying: events with consequences.
R. Hama bar Bisa returns after twelve years, meets his son unknowingly, is distressed, stands before him, and his wife rebukes him: a full narrative.
Something happened (a boat sank with two scholars) and Rabbi responded by permitting their wives to remarry: an incident followed by a ruling.
Rav Yosef son of Rava leaves study to go home; his father comes out armed to meet him, they quarrel, and both miss the pre-fast meal: actions, conflict and a consequence.
A couple comes before Rabbi; he has them bathed and fed, blood is found, and he rules: a sequence of events with a resolution.
A rumor scenario and a precedent that is only alluded to, with no incident actually narrated.
Bar Kappara fails to stand, R. Shimon takes offense and complains to his father, who answers him: an event, an emotional reaction and a response.
Mar Ukva's son reports on the pauper and Mar Ukva doubles the gift; on his deathbed he gives away half his wealth. Concrete actions with responses.
Ravina puts a halakhic question to Rav Ashi and gets an answer. Nothing happens beyond the question and the reply, and there is no conflict.
A report of Rav Ashi's blessing practice at a wedding, cited as precedent. Nothing follows from it.
A legal discussion of an incident at the wagons of Tzippori, but too little of the incident is given to make a story.
Only the opening of a paternity case before Rav Yosef, with both parties' claims. No event is narrated within the passage.
A purely dialectical exchange about a hypothetical deer on a Festival. There is no event.
The Bathsheba incident is only alluded to in a legal argument, and it is biblical in any case.
A negligent teacher is removed under a public vow by Rav Aha and later reinstated by Ravina because no better teacher was found: an incident with responses.
Rava plans to expound the Name publicly and an elder objects. This is speech only, but there is conflict and an implied change.
A couple comes before Rabbi; he has them bathed and fed, blood is found, and he rules: a sequence of events with a resolution.
A woman testifies before Rava that her husband died in a famine; his cross-examination of her leads him to change his ruling. An incident followed by a ruling.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna arrive in Hintzevu, are asked a question, debate it, and are corrected by Rav Idi. Mostly speech, with disagreement and a mild rebuke.
A renter takes a forbidden route, the donkey dies, and the case comes before Rava, who rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
Ravin the Pious goes to betroth a woman for his son and betroths her to himself. The Gemara's questions and answers around the act are commentary on that event.
A noblewoman tempts R. Tzadok, he climbs into the lit oven, and she relents: actions, conflict and a resolution.
Yehudit disguises herself, asks R. Hiyya a question, drinks an infertility potion, and later the matter is revealed and he responds.
A goblet deposited with Hasa, Hasa dies without instructions, and the parties come before Rav Nahman, who rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
A man sells land to Rav Pappa, no longer needs the money, and Rav Pappa returns the land: an incident and a response.
A certain man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags and Rav Shimi bar Hiyya examined it before Rav: an incident followed by a ruling. The Gemara's question after it is commentary.
Almost all speech: a question put to two rabbis and their answers. Rabbi Yehoshua's sarcastic exposure of the questioner adds conflict, but there is no action beyond the speaking.
A bare report that Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Ya'akov, cited as precedent inside a baraita, with nothing narrated.
Two men quarrel over a public office, come before Rav Yosef, Rav Adda bar Ahava argues for his host, and the host is appointed: a real incident with a resolution.
Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok's first-person account: the dry bread, the olives sent and declined, and the father's message back. The mishna and the Gemara's inference that follow are commentary.
Rav Hisda's statement about his own early marriage: a self-report with no incident.
A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment, the owner found him and spoke, and the brewer came before Rava for a ruling: an incident with a resolution.
A chain of hypothetical legal dilemmas. No event is narrated.
Rav Beivai visits Rav Yosef's house and, after eating, has the ladder removed from under him: a one-time incident with an action. It is framed by statements of law.
The passage holds only a fragment: the Galilean people sending a question to Rabbi Helbo. That is a quasi-speech act with no conflict; the rest of the exchange falls in the context.
A seating arrangement followed by a statement and a Gemara discussion: the Yevamot 17a case the expert ruled is not a story.
The orphan's wine was taken, rose in price, and the parties came before Rav Nahman, who ruled: an incident followed by a ruling.
A bill of divorce is found in Sura, the Sages search for the man named in it, and witnesses come forward: a real incident with a response.
After Rabbi Meir's death, Rabbi Yehuda bars his students; Sumakhos pushes in, Rabbi Yehuda grows angry and Rabbi Yosei responds. Actions, an emotion and conflict.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seek rulings from Rabbi Yohanan and then Reish Lakish, are threatened, and return to Rabbi Yohanan: a sequence of events with conflict.
A ma'aseh: a Madonite in Jerusalem wants to give gifts, acquires land, makes the transfer and dies, and the Sages fulfil his words. Several actions and a resolution.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa and the Angel of Death, his death, the pillar of fire, and Rabbi Alexandri's plea: a full narrative. The Abaye exchange at the end is attached commentary.
An old woman sells the orphans' ox, the relatives come before Rav Nahman, argue the case and receive a ruling: an incident with a resolution.
A habitual frame (weekly charity) followed by a one-time event: one day his wife delivers it and reports what she overheard.
A man tells his fellow that their pure foods became impure; the case comes before Rabbi Ami, who rules, and Rabbi Asi objects. An incident with a ruling and a conflict.
A certain man mortgaged his orchard, it aged after five years, and the creditor came before the Sages, who wrote him an authorization: an incident followed by a ruling.
A Roman courts a woman, makes her ill with pomegranates, then cures her: a sequence of actions with change. He is a post-biblical figure, so the story is in scope.
A creditor seizes the orphans' ox from a herdsman, the two dispute, and they come before Rav Nahman, who rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
Shmuel is helped off a ferry by a man who turns out to have a case, and Shmuel disqualifies himself: an incident with an action and a consequence.
Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav's testimony about the siege of Jerusalem and the Sages' rejection of it: an incident followed by a ruling. It is a Mishnah story, which R-C1 assigns to the Mishnah.
Habitual frame (R. Meir mocking transgressors) followed by a one-time event: Satan appears, he crosses the rope bridge, and is stopped and rebuked.
A certain man is slandered over his lineage and a rabbi rules on it; the incident-plus-ruling shape R-C0 admits.
Rav Nahman arrives and is asked a halakhic question, which he answers from a mishna; this is speech with no conflict and nothing following.
Rav Huna's ambiguous retort embarrasses R. Hiyya bar Avin and Rav Huna repairs it. The embarrassment is an emotional event, so this is more than a bare exchange.
Rav Kahana is tempted, throws himself from the roof, is caught by Elijah and given dinars. A full narrative, and Elijah appearing to a rabbi reads as in scope.
A report of Rav Ashi's practice for the wedding blessings, cited as halakhic evidence; nothing happens and no one responds.
Two conflicting deeds come before Rav Yosef, he rules, and the losing claimant protests and asks for a remedy; an incident with a ruling and a response. Segment 6 is the Gemara's own commentary.
The visit to the ailing Rabba bar Avuh frames what is mostly an exchange of questions and answers, with mild friction between Rav Huna and Rav Nahman. Segment 4 is the Gemara's analysis.
Rav walks among sheaves and makes a remark to them, followed by Rava's dictum; the act leads nowhere.
The Gemara's dialectical commentary on R. Ya'akov's incident, not the incident itself.
The opening of the narrative of Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi at King Izgur's gate, which continues into a full story.
A report of the Galileans' ongoing practice of buying a poor man meat, followed by the Gemara's explanation. Nothing happens beyond the practice.
Rav Aha bar Abba visits, places his great-granddaughter on his lap, and Rav Hisda challenges him; an action with conflict and a sharp exchange.
Abaye loses a donkey and exchanges messages with the Samaritans, who return it on account of his reputation; an incident that leads to an outcome.
The Talmud's baraita gives the sequel to R. Zekharya's Mishnah story: in response to the ruling he keeps his wife in a separate house. A response to an event, carried in the Gemara.
A virginity dispute comes before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi, who tests it with the maidservants and the wine barrel and rules; a full incident with a resolution.
Mostly a scholarly exchange: a challenge, a silence, then a trip to Rabba, who answers and calls the questioner quarrelsome. There is conflict but little action beyond speech.
Yeimar bar Hashu sends his agent to seize a dead debtor's boat and the rabbis confront the agent; an incident with a ruling.
Fire breaks out at a wedding, the bride cries out, and a burned man is found; a narrated event. Segment 3 is the legal discussion that follows.
A renter disobeys the owner's instruction, the donkey dies, and the case comes before Rava, who rules while Abaye disputes; the cow-case shape.
The Sages urge R. Abba bar Zavda to marry and he gives an excuse; a speech exchange without real conflict, followed by the Gemara's explanation.
A virginity dispute comes before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi, who tests it with the maidservants and the wine barrel and rules; a full incident with a resolution.
A report of what Rav Malkiyyu did (married off a deaf-mute and wrote a marriage contract), cited for Rava's praise and reasoning; nothing follows from the act.
While travelling, two rabbis see men sowing diverse kinds and argue over ostracizing them. The conflict is carried in speech alone and no action follows.
A chain of events: Rav Anan's letter, Rav Huna's insulting reply under threat of excommunication, Rav Sheshet delivering it, and Rav Anan consulting Mar Ukva, who rebukes him.
A man brings R. Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing; he refuses it, seats other judges, and is struck by his own bias. Several actions, and an inner reaction.
Homiletic exposition about fingers and ears, and a baraita. Nothing is narrated.
The passage only alludes to the Tzaidan incident ("etc.") and asks what the Mishnah means. The incident itself is not told here.
Aher sees Hutzpit's tongue dragged in the dirt, reacts, and goes out and sins. An event, a reaction, and a consequence.
A chain of hypothetical halakhic dilemmas. No event.
A narrated wonder incident: the mustard branch breaks, yields nine kav, and its wood roofs a booth. This is the open eyewitness-wonder edge, which the expert accepted on Ketubot 111b.
R. Yehoshua ben Levi visits Gavla and curses the land's fruit. The next year R. Hiyya finds the clusters shrunk and is sent away: a consequence follows.
A bare report that R. Yohanan issued a ruling, then the Gemara analyses the wording. No incident is narrated.
A divorcee comes before Shmuel, Rav Dimi tests her with her son, the baby recognises her, and she is ordered to nurse. A full incident.
An incident (a slave immerses a gentile woman for the sake of relations) followed by Rav Yosef's ruling and its grounds, plus brief parallel cases. This is the incident-plus-ruling shape.
Rav Ashi first fails to remember, later remembers and testifies, notices Rav Kahana's hesitation and responds. Several actions.
A study-hall scene: a teaching, a clamour of objection, and Rav Yosef's defence. Mostly speech, but with conflict.
A widow's claim against Rav Hiyya Arikha: a lawsuit, his refusal, a seizure authorisation, an appeal to Rava, and further rulings. A sustained narrative.
Rabbi falls ill, R. Hiyya visits and finds him weeping, asks why, and Rabbi answers. Illness, a visit and an emotional reaction.
A man bequeaths his property to 'Toviya' and dies, Toviya comes, and R. Yohanan rules. An incident followed by a ruling, though minimal.
A rumour of a betrothal circulates, the case is sent to Abaye, and he rules that the rumour is suppressed. An incident with a ruling as its resolution, though thin.
R. Yohanan hears that the Habbarim have reached Babylonia, shudders and falls, is told they take bribes, and sits back up. Emotional reaction and action.
Yudan's sons are freed, Rav Aha permits them to marry, and Rava challenges him. An incident followed by a contested ruling.
A narrated incident: a fox nests in a turnip, which is then weighed. It is a one-line wonder cited as evidence, the open edge of R-C5, so low confidence.
